utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning, Madam Plavsic. We were informed, although no written report is yet there, that you were medically checked this morning and that the result is that, although circumstances and some stress add to your high blood pressure, that medical reasons are not an obstacle for further testifying. This is just a summary. Also, in view of the fact that yesterday you expressed as your preference to go through this as quickly as possible, I suggest to you, but please correct me when I'm wrong, that we are in a situation now where you'd prefer to continue. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've said that the doctor has performed an examination. I understand that term to mean something else. He did come and measure my blood pressure, my contact with him lasted five minutes, and the blood pressure was 190 over 100. And from this conversation with him that lasted five minutes, I concluded, perhaps wrongly, that he had not had a look at my medical file. The file that I did not know would accompany me in the first place. It is in the Swedish language, and I had occasion to see from a distance that it's a rather thick file. He told me today that it is quite normal that I should have a high blood pressure under this kind of stress and then I asked him whether he had read my medical file, which is in Swedish, and he said he had. And from that file, one can conclude that this is my most serious medical problem even in Hinseberg. He continued to say that it is quite normal, that I am under stress and that this fact would pose no difficulty, and then I told him the following: "You are a doctor. I am not a free person. And you bear the responsibility." He asked me, "What would you do if you were free?" And I answered, "I would go to a hospital and ask to be examined." So that's the conversation that I had today with the doctor in the presence of a nurse. That is all I can tell you. As to how I feel, that does not matter much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I specifically, when asking to further look into the matter, I specifically have drawn the attention to the fact that the medical file came with you from Sweden and I suggested that the doctor would have a look at it. I do understand that you asked him whether he looked at it and that he confirmed he did. Now, are we -- are you in a position that you could testify in your own view at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you are putting this answer in my mouth. I stand by what I said yesterday. I don't know why -- this is a place where I have to say, maybe not for the sake of you who are present here, but also because of my family, it is not natural to have those waterfalls in your head, this clock ticking, that I have no concentration, that I cannot, when I walk, stick to a single direction. I did that in the hallway of the detention unit today to check, and finally I'm not an anonymous person, and I am saying this so that it be known. That's it. That's my answer to your question. And you can continue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Plavsic, given the circumstances, the Chamber thinks that we should calmly and slowly start, and whenever you feel uncomfortable, or perhaps I should say less comfortable or less -- more uncomfortable than you do now, please address me, if you find that there is any change in your ability to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On behalf of Mrs. Plavsic, I must object. Mrs. Plavsic has told you that she was seen by a physician for five minutes this morning and the only objective fact that has come out of that examination, the blood pressure test, is that her blood pressure is 190 over 100. Mrs. Plavsic is 76 years old. This is not her treating physician. He has not contacted her treating physician in Sweden. This is a man who saw her for five minutes, and yesterday another doctor or nurse here saw her for five minutes. You've heard her medical state and you can see her state as well, how it manifests itself, and her inability to focus and concentrate. I think I'm at liberty to say that my instructions from Mrs. Plavsic are that she is very apprehensive, that this will put her health if not her life in jeopardy. This is a very serious matter. High blood pressure at her age and this situation is very serious. We object to this proceeding. On another level, what could possibly be the value of evidence from a witness who has told you and you know her state and her health. So I think both from a medical point of view and from a legal point of view, both of which are legal matters, I submit, this is highly inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before considering what you've just said, we would like to hear from the parties, whether they would like to add anything or would like to make any submissions in relation to what was just said on behalf of Mrs. Plavsic. Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. While the Defence has the profoundest concerns about where we are, of course Mr. O'Sullivan is here to protect Mrs. Plavsic's interests, and it is Your Honours who have the responsibility of ultimately protecting Mrs. Plavsic in all the circumstances in relation to whether she should or should not give evidence and in what way and according to what timetable. And the Defence position, quite naturally, is that while we would make no submission that amounted to what in our judgement imposed any oppressive burden on a witness in this case, it's our function to protect Mr. Krajisnik. When one considers it from the position of Mr. Krajisnik, it is of the utmost concern that a lady who did, on any footing, occupy a very significant position in the events concerned, should be giving evidence in circumstances of extreme pressure, extreme pressure in the preparation, and I won't go into that in the presence of the witness but I do flag it up, and I would, if necessary, ask for the opportunity of making submissions on that in the absence of Mrs. Plavsic. The extraordinary inadequacies, in our submission, in the run-up to her arrival here to give evidence, now we have a situation where a medical report has been obtained, there is a lack of clarity. Although there are all sorts of figures in a medical report, we don't, for example, at the moment understand whether the doctor who briefly examined Mrs. Plavsic yesterday even reads Swedish and to what extent he or she is able to disentangle the medical information in a file in another language if he or she doesn't, we would submit that it would be normal in these circumstances that before the major step of embarking on Mrs. Plavsic's evidence is taken that a medical report following that examination should at the very least be available to the parties and to Mrs. Plavsic's counsel to be considered. The timetable that the Trial Chamber is contemplating for tomorrow, and in fact, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. O'Sullivan has jumped the gun by one day, she will in fact be 76 tomorrow, the timetable adopted for tomorrow is in our submission, prospectively --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 77. [In English] Sorry, sir, you know better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I had understood from the record, from the note that Mrs. Plavsic's date of birth was 7 of July, 1930. If I'm wrong about that, I think my arithmetic is okay based on that information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right, I am not right. Can you imagine in what kind of situation that I don't know how old I am. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, let's not make it a dispute between Defence counsel and a witness what exactly her age is. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Shall I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But before you do so, I don't think that a timetable has been finally set for tomorrow, although some inquiries were made as what would be possible and what would not be possible. I'm not aware of any decision taken in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll return to that in one moment, if I may. The -- what I said a moment ago just demonstrates how dangerous it always is to discuss a lady's age, and that's once more been demonstrated publicly. The -- so the -- on the prospective timetable, Your Honour, it is this: It is that we received express notification yesterday that the Court had set aside at least for prospective availability from 9.00 tomorrow until 7.00 tomorrow, so effectively a double day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I said there is no decision on tomorrow. And one thing is for certain: There will be no session from 9.00 in the morning to 7.00 in the evening. Would you please refrain from speculation where I clearly indicated that no decision has been made for this tomorrow. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm delighted to hear that, Your Honour. And I'm sure Your Honour can see the concerns that might have arisen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, what is important for Mr. Krajisnik is that any significant witness in this case, and let us assume that any witness now called is intended to be significant, should give evidence relieved of any extraordinary pressures. And the timetable -- and Your Honour, I'm afraid I do not resile from the comments I've made in relation to the prospective scheduling tomorrow because that is clearly linked to a wish to finish Mrs. Plavsic's evidence in accordance with travel arrangements, in accordance with days set aside to deal with other witnesses, and that is not right, Your Honour. It is not right that the parties should, once again, as we have seen with other witnesses, should be put under these inordinate pressures and the corner should be cut in relation to such important matters. It is simply not fair to Mr. Krajisnik. And in our submission, that requires the most careful reconsideration. So far as Mrs. Plavsic giving evidence at all is concerned, there was, and it was not necessary to pick it up at the time yesterday, but my B/C/S speaker in court yesterday, Mr. Jonovic, advised me that at one point when Mrs. Plavsic had said that she didn't know whether she could take it, that's to say the giving of evidence, in fact the sense of what she said was that she didn't know whether she could complete it. And this, to some extent, highlights precisely the concerns. In our, submission, the Court must not embark on any evidence of Mrs. Plavsic unless it is confident, within reasonable bounds of course, confident that that evidence will be completed and will be completed properly with the fair opportunity for the parties to deal with it at a fair pace, to ensure that the witness is not under undue pressure. And those are our submissions, Your Honour. It is too hasty to plough on into beginning Mrs. Plavsic's evidence without much more careful consideration than the Trial Chamber is currently giving.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just excuse me, Your Honour, just a couple of quick comments. First, with respect to the -- well, first I think it bears noting as must have been apparent, that Mr. Stewart was addressing himself to a number of issues, not the sole issue which I understood was before the Court with respect to Mrs. Plavsic's immediate fitness to proceed, and with respect to those aggregated submissions, I would simply note that the Prosecution understood, for example, that setting aside tomorrow for whatever sessions the Court deemed appropriate was not a signal in any way to anybody that the entire day or indeed any particular portion of the day would be consumed. I think the issue at the moment is one that was inferentially framed by Mr. Stewart and that is that the Court needs to make a determination within reasonable bounds, of timing, with reasonable bounds of objectivity, and information available of the timing for proceeding. And in that respect, therefore, the Court, I presume, will want to consider the information it has received concerning her medical condition, whether further information would be of assistance to the Court in reaching an objective and appropriate determination in that respect. I am confident -- first of all, I think we all realise that similar situations arise in courts around the world all the time. This matter can be dealt with in an appropriate way and I believe it will be. Finally I would say I'm not -- in terms of the aggregated submissions I referred to earlier, I'm not aware that there was any unusual process in place with respect to the witness herself in the projected schedule. The witness arrived, the Court began to move forward. Whatever preceded that appeared to me to bear only on issues related to the parties and the lawyers and not the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Mr. Tieger did go second and since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you get a short time. Please respond briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will deal with these important matters in as short a time as I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please refrain from commenting on where I give you some guidance as using less time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. But, Your Honour, what happened before Mrs. Plavsic arrived has clearly impinged upon the timing in this court. The very short time given for her to peruse and consider her draft statement, with her being, it appears, quite consciously deprived of the information she requested by way of transcripts of her interviews, led us to spend a considerable time in court yesterday doing work which should have been done before she arrived. The questions about tomorrow's schedule tie in with the important questions as to where are we going now in relation to the timing? If Mrs. Plavsic does give evidence, where are we going in relation to the timing of her evidence? How much time is to be spent doing what? What are to be the limits and what is contemplated? How are those limits intended then to be worked into the projected time available, if it is still intended that, come what may, Mrs. Plavsic is on her way back to Sweden on Saturday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. This Chamber will have to make a determination in which of course it will have to see what are medical risks which should not be taken and what are medical consequences of a situation of stress which is inherent to the present situation, taking into account all circumstances, such as age, such as the subject of the evidence to be given. We'll have to make a determination on that, and we'll have to do that taking into account all interests involved, that is the interest of the accused in this case, it is the interest of the witness herself, and it's also the interest of justice, which, of course, is not an interest other than Mr. Krajisnik's interest. It is an interest that all relevant information should be available to this Court, and if I say "all relevant information," we are all aware, of course, that we could spend easily 500 hours, a thousand hours, 2.000 hours, 3.000 hours, on finding all facts, all details, which are covered by this indictment. The Chamber will have to strike a fair balance on these issues, and we'll take a short break to do so. The Chamber might, given the circumstances, and given what you told us, Mrs. Plavsic, might also seek confirmation of information that was received, such as the -- and I just mention two issues, the time the examination took, but also, for example, whether the medical file which seems to be in a foreign language has been consulted and/or whether there has been any contact. If this brings us any new information, the Chamber will inform the parties about it. The Chamber will consider whether we'll then hear further submissions or whether we'll already give a decision and just inform the parties on this -- these matters. We'll have a short break, Mrs. Plavsic. We want to take some time to consider the present situation. We stand adjourned without a clear time for resuming, but the parties should remain standby. --- Break taken at 11.36 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has received a copy of an e-mail that was sent by Mr. McFadden to Mr. Petrov. I'll read it out to you. The Chamber has decided on the basis of this information and is not inviting any further submissions on the matter. The e-mail reads as follows: "The medical officer has reviewed her" which stands for yours, Mrs. Plavsic -- "which was sent here by her treating physician in Sweden. As a result of this, he found it necessary to monitor the blood pressure, her" which we read as your, Madam Plavsic -- blood pressure readings from high on admission to the detention unit and prior to her departure for court both days but the medical officer stated that they are not critical. He observed that her blood pressure was normal upon her return from court yesterday, leading him to conclude that the raised blood pressure was as a result of the stress experienced in the courtroom. He offered her medication to help alleviate this stress, which she refused. She continues on the medication regime she brought with her from Sweden. The Swedish medical report was translated for the doctor, who is fully aware of its content." That was the message sent to this Chamber. The Chamber has thoroughly considered all circumstances, the wide range of circumstances, involved in this case, from preparation, attitude of the witness, interest of the parties involved, everything, and we have decided that we'll cautiously continue with hearing your testimony, Madam Plavsic. May I then remind you, Mrs. Plavsic, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I also invite you to very much focus on the questions put to you and to focus your answers on what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mrs. Plavsic, have you received the corrected version of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have received it. I received it yesterday afternoon. I did not read it because I think we worked together here on those corrections, and if something was left out, when we come to it we can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the parties received a copy of it? Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we received yesterday afternoon a corrected version and then this morning a version which I -- just before we came to court. I'm not sure whether and to what extent the version received this morning differs at all from the one we received yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of two versions being distributed. What the Chamber has in front of it at this moment is a new version which clearly indicates the, as we call it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed that it is the same version and it has been presented in a way which would facilitate to find what changes there were. Is there any issue raised by the parties as to whether the -- what Mrs. Plavsic yesterday raised as matters to be corrected is not correctly reflected in a new version?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it may simply be an example, Your Honour, because we had thought and expected -- and we make no criticism of Mrs. Plavsic here, but we had thought and expected that in the quietness of not being in court she would be specifically reviewing her statement to ensure it was what she was willing to sign, and it would still be better if she had that opportunity. But, Your Honour, may I give an illustration of a specific concern in relation to and it arises on yesterday's transcript, if Your Honours have that. We have the continuous numbered version now, and this begins at page 26787, if Your Honours have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm getting it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do all Your Honours have this, by the way, as we go along? Because it's not going to be easy for Your Honour's brethren to follow this without the transcript up in front of him. I hope they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's at least in the middle, so they can join me in looking at my screen at this moment. Let's proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That doesn't look very easy from where I'm sitting, Your Honour, but no doubt it can be managed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm delighted to hear that, Your Honour, and for His Honour Judge Canivell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm delighted you're pleased and delighted, Your Honour. The -- Your Honours, it's page 26787 where we are dealing with paragraph 9 of the statement. Mrs. Plavsic said -- Your Honour, if at any point Your Honours felt that this should not appropriately be considered in the presence of the witness, then I wouldn't probably make strong submissions but I'm not suggesting anything different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we -- no, at this moment I think -- unless the Prosecution would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit, in principle, it's correct that she should be here because it is, after all, her evidence. She said: I have an objection or remark to make in relation to the first sentence. It says: I believe that Mr. Krajisnik had a very important role in the Assembly of Bosnian Serbs, and so on. And then she made it clear that - I'm summarising - it wasn't surprising because he was after all the president. But then she continued over the page, top of 26788, the second part: And the Supreme Defence Council, because without him it would have been impossible to do anything, his influence in the Supreme Defence Council was quite different than in the Assembly. And, Your Honour, I won't read every word. But then she goes on, at the bottom -- Your Honours see the gist of it. And then towards the bottom of that page, she says, well, and Your Honour, line 20 saying Madam Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm going to cut you short. I do see that on paragraph 9 you have some concerns. We are going to ask the witness to look at paragraph 9 in the new version whether that reflects --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's acceptable, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Plavsic, could I draw your attention to paragraph 9 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say straight away I got the point, I think. I said yesterday -- I said what I thought, that it was quite natural that the president of the Assembly had an important role in the Assembly. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invite you to read paragraph 9, to tell us whether the correction you suggested is reflected in the new text such that not whether there is any additional information to be given but whether the correction you wanted to make yesterday, whether you find this reflected in the new paragraph 9. You see there are two matters.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that here in paragraph 9, you put on the same footing of importance the influence of Mr. Krajisnik in the Assembly and in the Supreme Defence Council, which is not correct. Mr. Krajisnik is very important in the Assembly, whereas in the Supreme Defence Council he was the same as all the other members. So here in the corrected text it's still reads that his influence is equally important both in the Assembly and in the Supreme Defence Council, which is not correct, and I think I did say that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. While whether it reads, as you said, is still to be seen. But if it would help you out, if it would read, "I consider Mr. Krajisnik's participation in the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and although to a lesser extent in the Supreme Defence Council very important," if that would sufficiently express the distinction you'd like to make --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this. Your Honour is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm entitled to, Your Honour. I act for Mr. Krajisnik. I'm entitled to register an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You get one minute. I'm trying to get this statement such that it reflects the -- what the witness told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course there always could be said more words about it, and therefore I'm seeking to see whether there is a text which sufficiently reflects what the witness just told us. I'm listening very carefully to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can make a submission of one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One minute, Your Honour. Your Honour should leave it to the witness to make her amendments, Your Honour. This trouble -- this problem has been caused by doing it in consultation, as it were, between Your Honour and the witness yesterday, where the Defence registered its concerns that the witness was being steered. This is the whole problem about doing this statement in this way and having done it in court. Mrs. Plavsic should be invited quietly to go away and go through her statement and have the opportunity of making it her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is we've seen what happens if we leave it to Mrs. Plavsic. We have nine hours of interview which are, I would say, a good basis for an exercise we are doing at this moment which are not suitable for direct processing. Mrs. Plavsic, would it assist you if we would include here that the importance of Mr. Krajisnik although important was less important in the Supreme Defence Council? Because you wanted to make that distinction, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was visible, what could be seen and heard, is that his influence in the Supreme Defence Council was no different than from that of the other members. I really don't know how it came about that his importance in the Assembly and his importance in the Supreme Defence Council were placed on an equal footing. I know that fine points are very important, although this is not a finer point anymore. It's the essence, the substance. I really -- I'm not able to give you a wording. Maybe if you provide a wording, I can say yes or no. How would you phrase it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, perhaps since this seems to be the problem, if we would strike the reference to the Supreme Defence Council as a whole and what you told us about it, what you saw as a difference, is then not related anymore to the text but is just what you told us in court, which basically is that Mr. Krajisnik's influence in the Supreme Defence Council was as other members from the Supreme Defence Council. I suggest that we leave that out so -- "and the Supreme Defence Council," and then the words in B/C/S, take that out as a whole. Yes?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further submissions in this respect? That is, correctness of the corrections made. Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No further comment on this point, Your Honour. It's just we had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On any other point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A general point, Your Honour. It would probably be a good idea, we suggest, if Mrs. Plavsic were to take the opportunity this afternoon and this evening just to ensure that she is content with her statement but no doubt that will appear, we hope, as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any observation by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't had an opportunity -- well, we haven't taken the opportunity, if one existed, to go through a painstaking comparison, but it appears to us, based on the review we have conducted, that the version before the Court now conforms to -- in essence, to what was discussed in court yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Plavsic, we would like to give you an opportunity, of course we have read the transcript of your interview, we have seen how it was processed in such a way that it was put on paper as your statement, we heard yesterday the corrections you made. We tried to work them in as carefully as possible. We provided you with a copy now which clearly also reflects what was changed. Perhaps during the next break or perhaps this afternoon or this evening, you could just look at it and see whether it now reflects what you told us was wrong in the earlier statement and whether it now is corrected in a way you agree upon. May I invite you to do so and then we'll continue at this moment with further questions. Then I again would like to ask you to very much focus your answers on questions we put to you. Yes, Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me just tell you one thing. I think that the entire transcript of the interview should have been sent to me as Mr. Nilsson had said he would when he was in Hinseberg. When I told him, "What next," he told me, "I'll send you the transcript. On every page you should put your initials, if you agree, and amend if necessary." And I talked to him, and he told me, "I'm sending you a summary."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There must be some misunderstanding, but I can assure you, Mrs. Plavsic, that the parties have available to them the full transcript, which is in English, and if they would find any point where the summary would --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is in contradiction with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- although I -- where there is not proper basis for this statement, in the transcript of that interview, of which they have received an audio recording as well so they can check whether the transcript is correct, they will, without any doubt, draw the attention of the Chamber to any such matter. So to that extent, the parties will actively, from their own positions, check whether this summary finds its basis in -- and if we would have such submissions, and if we would need any further clarification from your side, we might even consider to ask further clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope Your Honours will bear in mind that of course the audio recording and the transcript are both equally useless to Mr. Krajisnik himself because unhappily really the interview was conducted entirely in English, thus depriving him of that opportunity. I hope Your Honours will simply bear that in mind as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll keep that in mind, Mr. Stewart. Mrs. Plavsic, I'd like to put a few questions to you and later on an opportunity will be given to both Defence and Prosecution to ask questions about it. The -- but before doing so and since some reference will be made perhaps to the statement as it stands now, I would like to have provisionally assigned a number to the witness statement in its corrected version with the track changes as it is given to the parties. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned C7, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mrs. Plavsic, in your witness statement, you indicated that Mr. Krajisnik was perceived by you and by others as a powerful man. You also said that -- and that's, I checked that in the transcript, in the original recording, that it was impossible to do anything, and the Chamber understands that this is expressed in the book you've written as well. Could you explain to us, perhaps by giving one or two clear examples, why you considered him and how you could see that he was a powerful man, as you said, without whom it was impossible to do anything? Could you give us -- perhaps without giving the whole story but perhaps one or two examples, focusing on how this power became noticeable to you?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a very powerful man. Thanks to his ability to be very practical and realistic, I think in certain matters he even dominated over the president of the Republic, Karadzic. How does a man become powerful? I think you must have given some thought to that yourself. Just let me finish, please. During the war, as regards foreign policy - and when I say "foreign policy," I mean the numerous meetings abroad related to various peace agreements - he was necessary and he was present everywhere. What talks were conducted there, I have no idea, because I never heard anything from them when they came back, apart from what they would say at Assembly sessions. So as far as that aspect of life is concerned, he was always present. As for our internal matters, internal territory, he was the president of the Assembly. He was in constant contact with the MPs, and not only MPs but also with municipal authorities. So how can somebody conclude what I concluded even without making the rational analysis that I made? His office was always full. After the signing of the Dayton Accords, during peacetime, more than half of the population of Sarajevo was withdrawing, but even during the war, everybody went to ask Mr. Krajisnik but also ask Mr. Karadzic. However, people probably thought that he was more practical, so they went to see Mr. Krajisnik rather. So that even an ordinary person could see that there were people waiting outside his office, and there were many people in his office, people from the local level. When there were talks with Mr. Milosevic, I was never there. I never saw Mr. Milosevic, except when he came to Mount Jahorina with the Vance-Owen Plan, but even then I sort of allowed myself to turn my back on him and not even greet him. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I stop you for a second and ask some clarifying questions? I specifically asked for examples. Until now, the examples were not yet very precise. But one of the things you said as that he was always there at international meetings, and he never informed you about what happened apart from the information he gave to the Assembly. Do we have to understand that, that you say he did not consult, he did not discuss with us, they just went on on their own, and that is a demonstration of the de facto power? Is that a correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you also used the plural because as far as I know -- actually, we are talking about the period until the end of 1992. Only in that period was I present. And that was until mid-October, that I was at Pale. We were physically separated when we were at Pale, also. I did not socialise earlier with Mr. Krajisnik so that I would be able to sort of say, in passing, "Momo, can you please explain to me what was going on in Geneva" or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you were physically separated. Just factual. Where were you? Where was Mr. Krajisnik? You were where?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these were some five rooms which were used as the Presidency, the Assembly, and I don't know, the only thing was that the actual government was at Jahorina. When the shelling of Pale began, I went to Jahorina and some others left too, while Mr. Krajisnik stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stayed where?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stayed where?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stayed at Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand when you say "we were physically separated," you say he was, after the shelling at least, he was in Pale, I was in Jahorina. You may notice that I'm trying to find very factual information. Another question. You said we never saw Mr. Milosevic when he met with Mr. Milosevic; only once you made an exception. Were you aware of other meetings Mr. Krajisnik had with Mr. Milosevic? So where you were not seeing Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never present. The first time I met Mr. Milosevic was after the signing of the Dayton Accords. Perhaps you will ask the question of how this was possible. I was very open, and I objected very much against the policy of Mr. Milosevic. I think that I was the only one that was openly in opposition, and I know that Mr. Milosevic even told Mr. Krajisnik -- actually, no, Mr. Karadzic, once that they would need to remove me from the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to take you back to what you said before. You said, "When there were talks with Mr. Milosevic, I was never there. I never saw Mr. Milosevic except when he came to Mount Jahorina with the Vance-Owen Plan, but even then I sort of allowed myself to turn my back on him and not even greet him." Which makes it clear you once were present when he was there, but you did not communicate with him apart perhaps in negative body language. Is that correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like it to be known that this was a period until the end of 1992, from the start of the war until the end of 1992. As a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I had the opportunity to see Mr. Milosevic, but this was before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He communicated with Mr. Izetbegovic, but I wasn't present so I don't know what the substance of the talks was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll put a very precise question to you in this respect, which is the following: You said, "When there were talks with Mr. Milosevic, I was never there." This answer, does that relate to 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the signing of the Dayton Accords. Because Mr. Milosevic signed the Dayton Accords, and in the meantime, I became the vice-president, and then after that, after the elections, president. I had to communicate -- well, it doesn't matter if I had to or wanted to. I don't think that that's so important. But, anyway, we are talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about 1992. So your answer implies or suggests that in 1992 there were meetings with Mr. Milosevic where you were not present but where Mr. Krajisnik was present. Is that a correct understanding of the implication of your answer?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were to ask me could you be 100 per cent sure, I would say that I would not be. I mean, I didn't accompany them, I didn't go to Belgrade, I didn't go into the building where Mr. Milosevic was, and I didn't sit there. So I really couldn't say. Maybe they went to Belgrade and sat with Milosevic and had coffee. I don't know. I'm trying in a way to draw a picture for you. This is not my personal knowledge, but it's that kind of knowledge. For example, I needed Mr. Krajisnik, and his secretary would say, "No, no, he's not there. He went to Belgrade. They are having a meeting with Mr. Milosevic," for example. I needed to see Mr. Karadzic, for example, "Oh, he's in Belgrade since two days ago." So in this way, is how it was, if you can understand me. When they returned, no one -- I had my own principle. If someone didn't want to tell me anything, I would ask once. The second time I would be very reluctant and uncomfortable asking, so I didn't do that. Especially because it was not necessary in what -- in my work. At the beginning of July, in the Presidency, I was entrusted with the humanitarian sphere, with contacts with the religions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Plavsic, I invited you to focus. I have some follow-up questions on just a few lines you gave. You said, "There were always people in his office, Members of Parliament." May I take it that you knew the assemblymen so that for that reason you told us that they were there? Is that correctly understood, that you knew them as persons and therefore you knew that assemblymen were in or around his office?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Members of Parliament are concerned, I would perhaps divide them into several groups. With some, I don't know for which reasons, I did communicate with some, I would just be on greeting terms, how are you and so on, and there were others that I did not communicate with. I knew them all by sight. There are some whose names I don't even remember. But this was 14 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you there again? You said you knew them all by sight. Is that to say that that allowed you to observe that it were assemblymen that visited him in his office, were in or around his office? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were waiting there, near the secretary's desk, they were probably waiting for their turn to enter Mr. Krajisnik's office. But I think that it was not just assemblymen. Many people wanted to speak to Mr. Krajisnik. You could put the question why this was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not put that question. But I first would like to put the question -- I am trying to find out what is exactly the basis of your knowledge. You said apart from assemblymen, also people from the municipalities. How did you know, how did you identify those persons as people from the municipalities? Did you know them? Did you know them by sight? Did you speak to them? Could you please answer the questions. Did you know them by sight, the ones you considered to be people from the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew very few people from the municipalities, because I wasn't in any of the SDS forums. I did have an SDS membership card. I was a member of the SDS, but I wasn't in any of the bodies. And I think that the local authorities favoured and perhaps exclusively requested that members of the SDS be in the local authorities. I couldn't maybe say that this applied to everyone. Maybe there were members of the local authorities who were not members of the SDS. But let me answer your question, how did I know. When the secretary told me, "You cannot go inside," because, for example, the president of the municipality of, I don't know, let's say the president of the municipality of Pale, or the president of the municipality of Vlasenica - I can't remember at this moment - "is inside," so that's how I knew. Sometimes the secretary would say, the president, that's how they addressed him, the president, "The president is busy." In that case, I didn't know who was with him in the office. Perhaps -- Mr. Krajisnik is a very open person, a communicative person, and people sensed that perhaps, and perhaps he was able to ask -- to carry out what they asked him to do, so perhaps this was something that became known, and people then would say, "Well, go and see Momo and he will arrange that for you." So I -- I hope that I have managed to perhaps illustrate how it was actually, how things were in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Chamber is seeking to know what actually happened so that what you give as a more general statement that we know better what made you state those things. You were talking about -- you said he was a powerful man and you gave an example of his attendance of international meetings. When you are talking about his powers, should we understand this as powers that would stay within the formal powers he had, or would that go beyond the formal powers of his position as president of the Assembly or any of the other formal positions he held? Did it stay within these formal powers or did you consider it to go beyond the formal powers?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't feel so comfortable because I have to give you the first example that has to do with me. I would gladly actually just bypass that. When the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed before the war, and this was on the 25th of October, 1991, the Assembly concluded that contacts -- and already at the time people were coming from different international organisations to the Presidency, to Republika Srpska. I have to say here that it was always strange why they were in contact only with the party chairman or presidents, whereas Bosnia-Herzegovina also had an assembly, a Presidency, a government. For example, Mr. Carrington, I think that he was the first one to visit, he had contacts -- all right. He had contacts with Mr. Izetbegovic. Mr. Izetbegovic was the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was the party president of the SDA party, the Muslim party, and he was also the president of the Presidency. Mr. Kljujic also was a member of the Presidency and a president of the HDZ. Mr. Karadzic was the only person who was the president of the SDS but did not have a state post or function. But still it was a bit strange to me why a man who would be coming from a traditionally democratic country, with strong institutions, would be talking to presidents of parties and not to institutions. But let me answer your question. When the Assembly was formed, of -- the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I said that was on the 25th of October, 1991, and I think at the first session, the Assembly concluded to entrust myself and Mr. Koljevic the task of contacting international representatives. I cannot remember who came but I remember Mr. Carrington well, when he came. So that was my assignment that I was given. Then, at that time, meetings intensified amongst the three leading parties, the HDZ, SDA and the SDS, although there was considerable conflict amongst them also at the same time. So the presence of the international factors led to them having meetings. And then at this Assembly session, I was assigned -- not just me, but I can't remember whether it was also Mr. Koljevic or someone else. It was probably also someone else. But anyway, that I would be in the group that would be establishing and maintaining contacts with the HDZ representatives and the SDA representatives. However, no one ever informed me that a meeting or meetings were being held. Sometimes they were even being held in the Presidency building. And sometimes Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, would come to my office, and I had the impression that they would just come as if they were waiting -- they were coming to a waiting-room, to await the beginning of a meeting. And since this happened two or three times, I would ask, "Why are you in the Presidency building?" Because I could see they didn't come to see me or for any other reason. And then they would say, "Well, we are having a meeting here with the representatives of the HDZ and the SDA." And I was surprised, in view of the assignments that I had been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your testimony to be that he, as a matter of fact, participated in the talks for which you were assigned to participate and not together with you but you not being invited and he would be there to participate in those talks. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You understood me correctly. I was looking for an opportunity. It was all risky, it was a very responsible job, so all I was trying to do was to be clear and that perhaps someone else was better at performing the jobs that the Assembly had entrusted to me, but all I tried to do was to keep the Assembly informed, and I tried to have the Assembly make a request that reports be submitted on who did what, so that in an indirect way I would be able to inform them, please don't think that I am the one who is actually implementing the tasks that you have entrusted me with. And that's when the war broke out. I stayed in Sarajevo, and I was looking for an opportunity to go to Pale, actually to flee to Pale. Yesterday we discussed this term, to walk there or flee there. And I was given the opportunity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, you answered my question.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore I would like to take you to your next -- to another matter. In your statement, you said, and this is related to the Presidency, what became the Republika Srpska Presidency, that Mr. Karadzic mentioned that it was important that this Presidency existed even if you would do nothing, and you said that this in your opinion was typical of how he saw the Presidency and how it worked, in your view. Could I first ask you, Presidency meetings, and try to focus exactly on what I'm asking you, how were the meetings called? Was it standard, well, let's say, every Monday, Wednesday, Friday, or were they called occasionally and how they were called? Try to focus on my specific question: How would you know that a Presidency meeting would take place?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presidency was formed on the 12th of May in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. I did not ask you how the Presidency was formed. I asked you how would you know that a Presidency meeting would take place? Did you get a letter? Was it on the basis of a schedule which was prepared well in advance? Did you receive a telephone call? How were you aware that the Presidency would meet?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way of receiving a written summons to meetings. When I fled to Pale on the 22nd of May, I was told that Presidency meetings were being held every day. I think at 11.00 or something like that. No, no, no. Earlier. So I consider that to be appropriate because it was a serious situation, it was war. So it was understandable that they were being held every day. As far as a summons was concerned, this is how it was. Either the secretary would inform us or actually the statement that it was held every day at such and such a time, the Presidency meeting, I would simply turn up at the hour, at the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were Presidency meetings held with approximately, so not perhaps with exceptions but approximately with that frequency? That means five, six, seven times a week?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was told that this would be every day. But then, in practice, it turned out that this was not actually every day, but sometimes the president of the Presidency would be chairing the meeting, sometimes he was not present, and Mr. Krajisnik was not there either, so there would be no Presidency meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As an average, in a month, how many Presidency meetings would, approximately, would that be 10, 15, 8? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be more frequent. Only if there was an interval when they were away abroad for, let's say, 10 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gave you -- I gave you different numbers, so if you say it was more frequent, I have to know was it more frequent than 15 times a month?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a month?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes it was, and sometimes it wasn't. I'm sorry, but I will say that you have this idea of an organised structure; for example, one in which I as a university professor worked in. But you receive a summons for a meeting, and traditionally you would know when, which day and what time this would be held. I was the dean of the faculty, so I know, and this is -- this is how I entered politics. And I was constantly surprised. And it's not only this Presidency; I was also in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sometimes you would have the impression that it was like the Bosnians say, a sit-down, a get together. You meet, then the coffee comes, and then finally you can just leave without actually knowing why the meeting had been convened in the first place. So sometimes I would remark to that effect at the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that it's a very small department of a minor university would be better able to organise a meeting. So that is why I'm unable to give you a direct answer to the question you put, but I have to give you a descriptive one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you just told us about these meetings, would that apply to the Presidency in 1992? Because you made reference to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question was focusing on the Presidency of what became Republika Srpska. Would this reflect -- did your answer reflect what happened in --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be clear about what I said. It applies to the Presidency during the war in 1992, but I'm telling you there was nothing binding even in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Maybe there was a conference room that was official, et cetera, whereas this was wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm focusing on the Presidency meetings during the wartime in 1992. Now, where you said, at the end, you would ask yourself why that meeting was called, does that mean that there was no agenda distributed prior to the meeting to start? Is that correct, or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct. You put it correctly. No invitations, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, as far as decision making is concerned, if any decisions were taken during such Presidency meetings, could you give us an impression on how that worked, but then in factual terms, so as to would someone say, "We have to decide on this and I suggest so-and-so" or how was a matter to be decided? How was it introduced? Did you, for example, introduce matters on which you considered it necessary that a decision would be taken?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you can imagine how many problems existed at the time and how many people came to raise problems, such as to the office of Mr. Krajisnik. Since I was in charge of the area that you know about, so I'm not going to repeat myself, I had problems with supplying electricity and water to Sarajevo, because they thought it belonged with the humanitarian affairs, so I said in the Presidency we have to repair transmission lines, because electricity comes from the Croatian territory, crosses over our territory. The switchboard is in Sarajevo, and we need to repair transmission lines. Today, it's very difficult to grasp this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You said something has to be done about electricity supply. What -- how would a decision be taken on that? Would you suggest a decision and then what was done? Was it by voting? Was it by consensus? Was it -- could you please tell us what then actually happened in such a meeting, but again in factual terms, please.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Winter was coming, there was no electricity in Pale, none in Sarajevo. That was a sine qua non. I knew that we would be unable to do anything without the presence of the UNPROFOR; they had to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again, because you are explaining --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain it to you any differently. Otherwise I'm afraid I'm not going to be able to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It won't be a long explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But nevertheless, you are explaining what the problem was about the electricity. Let's just assume there was a problem which needed to be resolved. Then what happened in the meeting? Yes.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not authorised to start talks with the UNPROFOR on my own. It couldn't be a decision of Biljana Plavsic. It had to be a decision of the Presidency, so I raised it at the meeting of the Presidency, and everybody accepted it very gladly and said, "Go on, Biljana, work on it." So henceforth, I worked on it, and the greatest problem was to find a repairman who would actually accept to climb up there with a sniper shooting all the time. So the solution we found, as I told you before, was that a crew of Croat, one Croat, one Muslim, and one Serb would go up together, because one Serb had already been shot at by a sniper. So from my line of work, I informed the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. You informed the Presidency, you were not authorised to do it yourself, and the Presidency agreed that a certain course of action would be taken, including measures as you explained to us. Now, when the Presidency agreed, was there ever a vote where there were different opinions and that you would say, "We have to put this to a vote," or was there never any voting?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. Let me tell you I'm just talking about my line of work which was humanitarian affairs. I never encountered any resistance of the Presidency -- because it was not only electricity, there was the problem of water, the passage for convoys. Convoys had to pass through our territory to reach --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- And the army had to be involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there again. So you said, on your issues, you actually never found -- you never encountered any resistance. Were there other subjects, and I just want you to name the subjects without at this time expounding on it. Were there other subjects where there was disagreement, or whether there was by whomever introduced, whether there was dispute, argument about how to proceed, how to resolve that matter? So could you tell us whether there were any such subjects and to give one or two examples of such subjects?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. The general impression that I have is that there were differing opinions but no disagreements. There were different opinions. I understood that to be good; that based on those differing opinions, we would be able ultimately to find an optimum conclusion. Whether it was really optimum only time could show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the answers you're giving now clearly suggest a kind of a collegial reaching, common shared views on which you would proceed. At the same time, we see in your statement, where you say what was the need of a Presidency at all, Karadzic and Krajisnik had made up their minds already, and that -- the answers you're giving now seem to contradict what you said in your statement and in your interview. Could you tell me whether I correctly perceived this contradiction and how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it can look the way you just put it. I gave you one example where it would be difficult to find a person who would say, "Ban that convoy, let them starve, or let them do without electricity. However, at that time, there were talks going on about very important issues. The Cutileiro Plan, I can't remember when it was rejected, but we were aware of some solutions built into the Cutileiro Plan, and you know that I never heard at a Presidency session what it was supposed to be. When the Cutileiro Plan fell through, the Vance-Owen Plan was already gaining some momentum, and in every plan there was the constitutional aspect of the solution for the Bosnia and Herzegovina and the territorial aspect of the solution. That was discussed by those who went over there, and you will agree that this is the main -- this was the main issue for that time. It was an acute issue. I don't want to underestimate the importance of electricity and water because they are indispensable to everyday living, but this was about the fundamental solution for the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And there were some other things. Let me tell you, I find it very difficult to reach some conclusions because I take my time checking and cross-checking. Maybe it's what I take from my profession. But the general impression that I have, and it's not only my impression, that only two persons were deciding everything. I had that objection and I voiced it publicly before the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Why not say it now? Maybe I wanted too many confirmations of that. So it was not before October that I said it at the Assembly session in Prijedor. And at the National Assembly, the language used by Mr. Koljevic was, I believe, very true when he said, "Let's stop playing this game of collective mimicry."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred to the constitutional issues and the territorial issues, that on these matters, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were the ones who, as I understood you, proceeded in their own way without discussing the matters with you and the Presidency. Is that correctly understood? And I'll put another question to you.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I wouldn't say that it was a 100 per cent personal issue. It was not the issue of the Presidency but it was not 100 per cent an issue of personality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you the following: When you're referring to territorial aspects, do I understand you well -- would that mean what territory should be claimed in negotiations, or how do I have to understand the territorial aspects? Is that -- could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you analyse -- I don't know how many of those agreements existed. One of them, let's say, was accepted and that's the way Bosnia and Herzegovina is designed today. But each of those proposals had a constitutional solution and a territorial solution included. Proposals varied, but they had one thing in common and that was separation. It began with the Cutileiro Plan. According to the Cutileiro Plan, Bosnia and Herzegovina was cantonised, and out of those cantons, in the following plans, there were fewer and fewer separated parts until finally, in the Dayton Accord, Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided into two entities. As for the constitutional solution, the main problem was always to what extent the centralised authority would be strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on the territorial. What you are describing, I understand, is more or less on how maps were developed, what would be territory of what unit, and where you said earlier that on these both aspects, and they more or less proceeded in their own way, do I have to understand that that -- the maps and the development of those maps were not collegially discussed in the Presidency and that they would just take part in the negotiations or were they discussed? Did -- and you put them together, Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. Did they consult with the others before going to such conferences, for further negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not within the Presidency? That means with Mr. Koljevic and with you and --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about Mr. Koljevic because Mr. Koljevic did go occasionally. Mr. Buha, I believe, always went, as a matter of course. I cannot really say because I didn't even know when they were leaving and when they would come back. Of course, I'm only speaking about myself, about my knowledge. I'm trying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were not consulted on these territorial matters?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was trying -- I was not a member of the Assembly. I had the right to attend Assembly sessions, ex officio, without the right of voting, but with the right of speaking. Those were my rights in the Assembly. And even after 1992, when I was in Belgrade, I went to Assembly sessions to get some information, because of course I was interested in what was going to become of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was the only place where I could get what I hoped to be good information, to the extent that it was available to the assemblymen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you allow me one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, we have some practical problems as well. I suggest we had a relatively late start, that we have a short break now and then continue but only for a very short period of time; that would mean for not more than some 20 minutes after the break. We would then conclude at approximately 2.00, so that's 40 minutes from now, and part of that taken by break of anything between 15 and 20 minutes, and would that be too much for you or you would say, after break of little bit over quarter of an hour, another 20 minutes would do, and then we finish for the day?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll have a break until most likely 20 minutes to 2.00 and then continue only for another 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. In your e-mail this morning, or this afternoon that you read out, you mentioned that the -- Mrs. Plavsic's medical report had been translated. Can we request that you ensure that Mrs. Plavsic and I receive the translation of that medical report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Translation, has been translated, might be an oral translation. I'll inquire into whether there is a written translation, and if there is a written translation, I think that nothing would oppose you receiving a copy of it. Yes. Mrs. Plavsic, first of all, did you already look at the statement, the redacted statement, or did you not yet find time to look at it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have received a copy?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll leave that until perhaps later so that you have an opportunity to look at it first. Mrs. Plavsic, I'd like to take you to another subject. In your statement, you said that Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik decided everything, and therefore there was no need for a Bosnian Serb Presidency or any other state institution. We've heard some answers from you in that respect. In your book, "I Testify," you further explain that Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik made sure that only their supporters would remain in the leading positions. First of all, I'd like to ask you, the book you've written, and you have drawn our attention to certain pages of that book, what we find in that book is -- does that reflect truthfully what your recollection is on what happened at the time?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The first page of the book is not part of the actual contents of the book. It's the forward, and there -- excuse me just for a minute, please. I have the book here. I wrote there that the name of the book is very binding, as far as I'm concerned. That's why I called the book, "I Testify." And I said it is as if I had given an oath that I would speak the truth, only the truth, so help me God. And that's what also kept like a thread appearing throughout this book and also the second book. I'm talking about the events known to me in 1992, and then the second book covers the period from 1993 until 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are under some time restraints. I understand your answer to be that this -- that you confirm that what you've written in that book reflects what is the truth, and as you said, even under oath you would have written the same. Is that correctly understood? Then I on page 264, you said: "Everybody who was not Radovan's or Momo's man had to leave very soon." Could you give me one or two examples of persons --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you an example right away. For example, the example of the Prime Minister, Branko Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Branko Djeric, a prominent professor of the faculty for economics in Sarajevo, and is a person whom I believe to be a good patriot, who in such critical times sacrificed himself by taking on himself that post. So from my point of view, he was an exceptionally skilful person, an expert in his field, a man who knew the times were hard and even harder times were coming and it would be impossible to predict how hard the times would be, and in such a situation, he took this task upon himself. That man did as he believed a Prime Minister should work. He had a ministerial cabinet, and it's quite normal that the ministers were responsible first of all to him and then the entire government and Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, and I'd like to -- you to focus rather than on describing what you would expect a Prime Minister to do, what made you believe that Djeric had to leave because he was not Karadzic -- Radovan's or Momo's man. So you suggest that it was under their influence that he could not continue. Could you explain that specifically?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably their criteria; we have to have our own man. But in that sense, Mr. Djeric was a person of the Serbian people, a person who represented the interests of Republika Srpska in his own domain, in the same way that I was a member of the Presidency. I was not Krajisnik's or Karadzic's person, and I was not a member of the Presidency because of Krajisnik or Karadzic. And in the same way I assume that Mr. Djeric was not somebody who took upon that difficult post because of Karadzic for the reasons that I stated previously. So how did this manifest itself? For example, two ministers who at the time -- well, all right. They were important in peacetime as well, but you will understand that at that time the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Internal Affairs did have things to do. Let me put it that way. They said publicly to Branko Djeric in a quite rude way, in my opinion, "You are not our boss. We report to Karadzic." I was present when this was said. Mr. Mandic, in particular, had a manner like that. I was irritated by this disrespect towards a respectable, prominent figure. So instead of being happy to be even near him and to work together on the same job, they were disrespectful to him in that way. And I think that all of these signals were something that Mr. Djeric could not really take. He didn't have the protection of Mr. Karadzic. Now, this is my personal opinion. Quite to the contrary, there were suggestions addressed to Mandic that he should make such statements, and the threshold of dignity was crossed so that Mr. Djeric could take it no longer and he gave his resignation at the Assembly in Zvornik. I often heard the term "our man." When I analysed that it was not of a man of the Serbian people or of Republika Srpska but personally, a man of another man who wanted to implement his own policies through this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you there for a second? You describe more or less, although perhaps suggested by others, that it was the rude way Mr. Djeric was treated by the Minister of the Interior and by the Minister of Justice that that caused him to leave. In view of my question, and in view of the answer you gave, should I understand this to be that Mr. -- the Minister of Justice, Mr. Mandic, as you said, and the Minister of the Interior, that those were Radovan's and Momo's men opposed to Mr. Djeric not qualified as such?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer, Mrs. Plavsic. I'd like to touch upon another issue. In your witness statement you said, and I'm moving to a totally different subject, that all tactical decisions were taken by General Mladic. Could you tell us who took the strategic decisions? And, of course, we are talking about the army, the VRS.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never present during conversations, and I didn't see any orders that Mr. Karadzic as Supreme Commander, because the civilian authority should be above military authority. I don't know if I'm expressing myself well. But I never had the opportunity to see an order. Now I'm talking about the period of 1992. I've seen many orders after I was brought to Scheveningen, a pile of orders, which could be analysed in the same way that I analysed yesterday page 1 of this text. But what I can say is that I did not have the opportunity to see that, just like when you read -- well, I'm not going to go back to Napoleon. But, for example, there were many wars on our territory. Memoirs were written about World War I. And I know, for example, General Misic, when he received an order from Prince Aleksandar you could see the line or the chain of command very clearly. I think that's -- you would -- that's how you would describe it. But as for the personality of General Mladic, I think that I am somebody who is familiar with that. I've written about him, not chronologically, but I did write about some events, so I perhaps noted down some of my remarks. A book has now come out about General Mladic by a man whom I don't know, but who has known him since even from before the war. Allow me to finish, please. And all I can say is that he also is of the view that this is a man of such a character or nature that it was very hard to order him to do anything. If I were to tell you that at that time someone who did not respect orders in peacetime in the Yugoslav People's Army, which was a party army, I think that's how it was, I guess in all of those communist countries, if he was punished and you know the kind of punishments they had, he would be transferred somewhere, to Bitolj or somewhere to the border, and he was walked all over the territory, I was surprised, I didn't ask anyone but I knew how the system functioned, and I assumed that this was a stubborn man. When I got to know him and in the relationship that you are now interested in that we are talking about, I knew that a man really couldn't change. He's a very strong personality. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I'm going to interrupt you because it's not a real answer to my question, but perhaps I should rephrase it. But I do understand that your testimony is that the character of General Mladic was such that it would not be easy to keep him under control. But I was specifically, since your statement deals with tactical decisions, I was specifically drawing your attention to strategic decisions. First of all, are you familiar with strategic objectives adopted by the Bosnian Serb Assembly? These are six strategic objectives that even were officially published at a later time. Are you familiar with what I call six strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what a strategy is, but believe me, I don't know about these objectives. But it's been 14 years since those events. I don't know. I know what my objective was and what the objective was of the Serbian people. First, that we don't get killed, that 1941 doesn't happen all over again; that was a main objective.
