And so that we become a constitutive people in a country in which we have been living for hundreds of years. I don't know about those six. Maybe some I did know about at the time but really, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Plavsic, a last question for today will be put to you by Judge Hanoteau who is sitting to my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Plavsic, in your interview, you mentioned the role played by the personnel committee of the SDS. Do you recollect having spoken about this?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, in your interview.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, but I know that I also mentioned that in the book, too. Everything that happens on this planet of ours that interests us depends on the people. It depends on the people. If you have capable, and let's say honest, people in the relevant posts, it's still not a guarantee that things will proceed in the optimal way. It all depends on that. The communists understood that best, the importance of a cadre or a personnel commission. If you have your own man at a certain position, unfortunately for them it was important to be loyal to the Communist Party and not whether somebody was capable or not. In my work I experienced some quite terrible things from the personnel commission. They were not interested in whether I was an able professor and an educator but whether I was politically active or not. So since this is something that affected me, I have a dislike for personnel commissions. I think this is something that was copied from those times. We emerged from communism and then immediately the things we are talking about now came upon us, and I do have a dislike, and I must say that when they implement the personnel policy, they raise up the unfit, they destroy the honest people, because honest people you cannot manipulate and you cannot implement such a policy using them. So I probably mentioned the personnel commission in those terms, the cadre or the personnel commission decides who will be placed in which post. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Plavsic, please, can you confirm that Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were members of this SDS personnel committee?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who members of the Main Board were or the Executive Board, and I wasn't even interested in the party at all. I didn't have any party experience because you can seldom find a person who was at the university but was not a member of the Communist Party, not because they believed in communism but simply because that helped them to get ahead. So I can say as a direct answer to your question nothing could have happened without them, whether this person will be in this post, whether he will get this function or that function. I did not attend, nor do I know who the members of the personnel commission were, what they decided on. But from my experience I know that this is something that would not have been done without them. Who was in that post, who was in that post? They said, we have to appoint our own people. Very often, these people, our people, quote/unquote, are not exactly people that I would consider to be our people. I didn't have any posts in the SDS. I had a piece of paper which said that I was a member of the SDS. Therefore, I did not attend those meetings. All I can do is conclude. For example, I remember Branko Ostojic. Nobody knew him, a man who was supposed to be the Deputy Prime Minister. He was not there. Nobody knew him. And I asked Karadzic, "Who is this man?" Previously, our people came from Sweden. They came to me and said to me, "This Branko Ostojic," whom we know very well, "is supposed to be the Prime Minister." So I, as a Presidency member, had no idea about that. And I went -- they expressed themselves very negatively. I think the law in Sweden had some problems with him. I think that I good-naturedly warned Karadzic. I said, "Why are we dealing with such people?" I said, "Who is that person?" And he said, "Well, it's that guy there in the corner." Perhaps that can give you an illustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is to say that you said, Mr. Karadzic knew the man well and supported his candidacy to become Deputy Prime Minister. You -- the question was about Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He put him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Plavsic. We'll finish for the day. Perhaps -- we would like to see you back tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still alive. I'm still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Plavsic, we would like to see you back tomorrow morning, and may I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and neither about testimony still to be given in the future. Could we ask the security to escort Mrs. Plavsic out of the courtroom? I asked security to escort you out of the courtroom and we would like to see you back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at all circumstances relevant for these kind of decisions, the Chamber -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has decided that tomorrow the parties will be in a position to put questions to the witness, and this has been scheduled in the following way: The sequence is as we established earlier for Chamber witnesses, that is Prosecution first and then Defence. Tomorrow one-third of the time available during tomorrow's session, that is one hour and 20 minutes, will be available for the Prosecution; and two-thirds of the time will be available for the Defence tomorrow, that's two hours and 40 minutes. That's the way in which we'll proceed tomorrow. We adjourn until tomorrow morning -- Yes, Mr. Tieger, it seems that if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that the Court's decision reflect the particular circumstances. I just want to observe consistent with that, that the Prosecution may clearly have some questions in response to issues raised by the Defence. We'll obviously try to keep all of our -- any questions we have within the allotted time, but in terms of the order, clearly some issues may arise in response to questions posed by the Defence and so we wanted to bring that to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- I do understand that you'd like to have an opportunity to raise any further issues. We'll see what happens tomorrow. I don't know whether you would use all your time, I don't know whether the Defence will use all its time. We will proceed on the basis of this, and then see where it ends. And as I said before, there is no question about starting at 9.00 in the morning and going on until 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, the Defence has a brief submission as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We are very pleased to hear that last remark, thank you. The -- it is objectionable, in principle, we say, for the Prosecution now in the light of that ruling to indicate that they would want and for them to be given then an opportunity to respond and ask further questions after the Defence. So we put down that marker straight away, Your Honour. May I only add this, Your Honour. That there is the usual issue, if I might call it that, about an opportunity for Mr. Krajisnik himself to ask questions, as the Trial Chamber wishes us to do. We are going to see Mr. Krajisnik this afternoon. We will discuss that as an item on our agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, you are aware what the principles are that are applied; that is, that Mr. Krajisnik should first address counsel and see whether in the usual way, through representation, whether questions could be put to witnesses, and if there is any issue remaining which for -- after having consulted with counsel are not questions that could be easily put by counsel, then we always allowed Mr. Krajisnik certain questions. At the same time, you will be aware that in view of what both this witness has said about her relationship with Mr. Krajisnik and in view of what Mr. Krajisnik, although quite a long time ago, said about this witness, that this is a very sensitive issue and that if such questions would be put, that the Chamber would be very strict in applying what I would say, professional rules that are applicable, that means the way of behaviour of a party, if a defendant -- if an accused is representing himself, which is not here the case, then you know that he's under a strict obligation to apply rules of legal practice applicable to counsel as well. We do not disallow questions to be put by Mr. Krajisnik, but we'll be very, very strict on this aspect, in view of this witness, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I say that's most helpful to that -- in advance of our meeting with Mr. Krajisnik this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would go any other way, if we would not follow acceptable legal practice in a courtroom, we would stop immediately any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we well understand the principles. Thank you for that, Your Honour. And, as I say, it is very useful to have that guidance. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One last issue, Your Honour, that may assist both parties in examination. That is the following: It appears to the Prosecution that the excerpts from the book have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I had forgotten that, as a matter of fact. I have to make two observations. First of all, a provisional number has been assigned to the witness statement. The witness statement still reads that it's confidential. That should be different, since we have discussed the matter completely in open court. So that should be redacted for other reasons and independent from what Mrs. Plavsic thinks about it. We have referred to the book at this moment. Madam Plavsic has referred to passages of the book as well. For that reason, the registrar is now invited to provisionally assign a number to the portions of the book referred to, the pages of the book referred to, by Mrs. Plavsic, but as it stands now, only the pages that she referred to in her initial statement because the latter pages having been translated only very recently. I add to that immediately that Mrs. Plavsic testified about truthfulness of the book and that I could not understand the difference from covering the whole of the book, but we'll later see whether under this provisionally assigned number we would include the other pages as well. That has perhaps also got something to do with relevance, and the parties are invited to -- of course we will later discuss, I take it, admission of this evidence when it comes to a decision in that respect. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be C8, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: C8, pages of the book, "I Testify" from Madam Plavsic; and C8.1 the translation of the pages. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of July, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
